The '''jackfruit''' or '''jakfruit''' ('''''Artocarpus heterophyllus''''') is a fruit tree in the [[mulberry]] family of [[Moraceae]]. Native to India, the species was first described under the name ''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' in ''Encyclopédie Méthodique, Botanique'' in 1789 by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]], based on a specimen collected by botanist [[Philibert Commerson]].

The jackfruit tree is a large [[evergreen]] tree that can grow up to {{cvt|30|m}} tall. It has a dense foliage with leathery leaves which are smooth on one side and rough on the other. Fine hairs cover various parts of the tree, and the bark and leaves produce a sticky, milky [[sap]]. The tree is [[monoecious]] and produces an inflorescence consisting of cluster of small, pale green flowers from the trunk and large branches. The tree produces the largest of all tree-borne fruits, measuring up to {{cvt|90|cm}} in length and {{cvt|50|cm}} in width and weighing up to {{cvt|50|kg}}. The yellowish-green fruit has a thick shell with numerous [[tubercle]]s and emits a characteristic odour on ripening. The interior of the fruit consists of several yellow coloured fleshy bulbs each of which encloses a single seed.

The jackfruit tree might have originated in the [[Western Ghats]] range in India. In addition to the various countries in [[South Asia]] and [[Southeast Asia]], where it is extensively grown, it has also been introduced across parts of Africa, Americas, and Oceania. Though it grows on a variety of habitats at low altitude, it prefers moist, well-drained soils and sufficient sunlight. The tree matures and may start bearing fruits anywhere between 4 to 14 years and can have a productive lifespan of more than a hundred years.

The fruit bulbs and seeds are edible, and can be eaten raw. It is also sold canned or frozen, or processed into other foods. It is commonly used in [[South Asian cuisine|South]] and [[Southeast Asian cuisine|Southeast Asian]] cuisines.

==Etymology and taxonomy==
The name ''jackfruit'' comes from [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] {{lang|pt|jaca}} first mentioned by physician and naturalist [[Garcia de Orta]] in his 1563 book {{lang|pt|[[Colóquios dos simples e drogas da India]]}}.<ref>{{citation |title=Jackfruit |work=[[Oxford English Dictionary]], Second Edition |year=1989}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |year=2000 |url=http://www.bartleby.com/61/33/J0003300.html |title=The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language: Fourth Edition |publisher=Bartleby |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051130162835/http://www.bartleby.com/61/33/J0003300.html |archive-date=30 November 2005 }}</ref> {{lang|pt|Jaca}} is derived from the [[Malayalam]] word {{lang|ml-Latn|chakka}},<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/jackfruit |title=Jackfruit |work=[[Merriam-Webster]] |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=18 May 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518073857/https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/jackfruit |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Pradeepkumar |first1=T. |last2=Jyothibhaskar |first2=B. Suma |last3=Satheesan |first3=K. N. |date=2008 |editor=K. V. Peter |title=Management of Horticultural Crops |series=Horticultural Science Series |volume=11 |location=New Delhi, India |publisher=New India Publishing |page=81 |isbn=978-8-189-42249-3 |quote=The English name ''jackfruit'' is derived from Portuguese {{lang|pt|jaca}}, which is derived from Malayalam {{lang|ml-Latn|chakka}}, }}</ref> which is used to refer to the fruit in the [[Malabar Coast|Malabar region]] of India as mentioned by [[Hendrik van Rheede]] (1636–1691) in the third volume of {{lang|la|[[Hortus Malabaricus]]}}.<ref name=jordanus>{{cite book |first=Friar |last=Jordanus |date=1863 |title=Mirabilia descripta: the wonders of the East |url=https://archive.org/stream/mirabiliadescrip00jord#page/13/mode/1up |publisher=[[Hakluyt Society]] |page=13 |access-date=23 November 2012 }}</ref> It is derived from the [[Proto-Dravidian]] root {{lang|dra-Latn|kā(y)}} meaning fruit or vegetable.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9i2WeeTjmKwC&q=cakka+&pg=PT352 |title=Linguistic Archaeology of South Asia |first=Franklin |last=Southworth |date=2 August 2004 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |via=Google Books |isbn=978-1-134-31776-9 |page=352}}</ref>

In 1984, [[Ralph Randles Stewart]] suggested that it might have been named after botanist [[William Jack (botanist)|William Jack]] (1795–1822), a Scottish botanist who worked for the [[East India Company]] in [[Bengal]], [[Sumatra]], and [[British Malaya|Malaya]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stewart |first=Ralph R. |author-link=Ralph Randles Stewart |year=1984 |title=How Did They Die? |journal=Taxon |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=48–52 |doi=10.2307/1222028 |jstor=1222028 |bibcode=1984Taxon..33...48S |url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/149689/1/tax02453.pdf |hdl=2027.42/149689 |hdl-access=free |archive-date=31 March 2021 |access-date=23 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331125344/https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/149689/tax02453.pdf;jsessionid=88086FAD2AD5FB43E4E90FA71285E7A8?sequence=1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In India, it is known as {{lang|ta|palaa}} in [[Tamil language|Tamil]], {{lang|hi|kathal}} in [[Hindi]] and [[Bengali language|Bengali]], and {{lang|mt|phanas}} in [[Marathi language|Marathi]].<ref name="Names">{{cite web|url=https://www.goethe.de/ins/in/en/sta/pun/current-projects-/--/artocarpus-heterophyllus.html|title=''Artocarpus heterophyllus''|publisher=[[Goethe Institute]]|access-date=1 June 2026|archive-date=14 June 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260614222713/https://www.goethe.de/ins/in/en/sta/pun/current-projects-/--/artocarpus-heterophyllus.html|url-status=live}}</ref> It is known as {{lang|ms|nangka}} in [[Tagalog language|Tagalog]],<ref name="Morton">{{cite book |last=Morton |first=Julia F. |year=1987 |title=Jackfruit. In: Fruits of Warm Climates |url=https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/jackfruit_ars.html |publisher=Center for New Crops & Plant Products, [[Purdue University]] |pages=58–64 |isbn=978-1-626-54976-0 |access-date=21 May 2025 |archive-date=10 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310151710/https://hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/morton/jackfruit_ars.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and {{lang|ceb|nangkà}} in [[Cebuano language|Cebuano]] and in [[Malay language|Malay]], all from the [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian language family]].<ref>{{cite web |year=1972 |title=Nangkà |work=Dictionary of Cebuano Visayan |url=http://gutenberg.ph/previews/wolff/WCED-complete.pdf#page=776&zoom=auto,-76,270 |last=Wolff |first=John U. |volume=2 |page=698 |access-date=6 February 2020 |archive-date=26 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210226135218/http://gutenberg.ph/previews/wolff/WCED-complete.pdf#page=776&zoom=auto,-76,270 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2010 |title=Loans: jackfruit - ''Artocarpus spp.'' |url=https://acd.clld.org/formsets/29865 |access-date=17 July 2023 |work=Austronesian Comparative Dictionary |publisher=[[Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology]] |archive-date=17 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230717072821/https://acd.clld.org/formsets/29865 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is known as {{lang|th|khanun}} in [[Thai language|Thai]], {{lang|km|khnor}} in [[Khmer language|Khmer]], {{lang|lo|may mi}} in [[Lao language|Lao]], and {{lang|vi|mit}} in [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]].<ref name="Morton"/>

The species was first described under the name ''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' in ''Encyclopédie Méthodique, Botanique''in 1789 by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]], based on a specimen collected by botanist [[Philibert Commerson]].<ref name="Lamarck"/> The genus name ''Artocarpus'' is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]] words–'artos' meaning bread and 'karpos' meaning fruit.<ref name="Flora">{{cite web|url=https://www.efloraofgandhinagar.in/tree/artocarpus-heterophyllus|title=''Artocarpus heterophyllus''|publisher=[[Government of Gujarat]]|access-date=1 June 2026|archive-date=9 September 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260909134513/https://www.efloraofgandhinagar.in/tree/artocarpus-heterophyllus|url-status=live}}</ref> The species name ''heterophyllus'' means "variously leaved" in [[Latin]].<ref name="Names"/> It is part of ''[[Moraceae]]'', commonly known as [[mulberry]] family.<ref name="TBA">{{cite web |url=http://www.tropicalbiology.org/research/dip/species/Artocarpus%20heterophyllus.htm |title=''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' |publisher=Tropical Biology Association |date=October 2006 |access-date=23 November 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120815013508/http://www.tropical-biology.org/research/dip/species/Artocarpus%20heterophyllus.htm|archive-date=15 August 2012 }}</ref> It was placed in ''[[Urticaceae]]'' in the [[Bentham & Hooker system]] of classification by [[George Bentham]] and [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]], but was later reclassified under Moraceae.<ref name="Names"/>

==Description==
[[File:Stem of jackfruits tree.jpg|thumb|upright=0.6|alt=A jackfruit tree trunk|Trunk showing greyish-brown colouration]]

The jackfruit tree is an [[evergreen]] tree that grows up to {{cvt|30|m}}.<ref name="DNP">{{cite web |url=https://www.dnp.go.th/botany/eflora/floraSpecies.html?tdcode=04557 |title=''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' |volume=11 |year=2013 |page=341 |work=[[Flora of Thailand]] |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=9 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260909230210/https://www.dnp.go.th/botany/eflora/floraSpecies.html%3Ftdcode%3D04557 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="NP">{{cite web |url=https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/7/2733 |title=''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' |work=Flora and Fauna Web, [[National Parks Board]] |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=15 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251115153836/https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/7/2733 |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[bark (botany)|bark]] is hard and rough, and covered with scales. It varies from greyish brown to dark grey in colour.<ref name="NP"/> Twigs arise from the trunk, and are {{cvt|2 to 6|mm}} thick, with minute flattened hairs covering their surface.<ref name="DNP"/> The foliage is denser when the tree is young, and it spreads out when the tree grows further.<ref name="NP"/> The leaves are [[Alternate leaf|alternately]] and spirally arranged.<ref name="DNP"/>

The leaves contain three lobes in young trees, and become [[ellipse|elliptical]] or [[obovate]] in shape later. The [[lamina (botany)|lamina]] measures {{cvt|4 to 15|cm}} and {{cvt|2 to 8|cm}} across the longer and shorter axes.<ref name="DNP"/> The thin and leathery leaves are smooth on one side and rough on the other side.<ref name="NP"/> The leave surfaces has smooth hairs with the distribution sparser on the rough side. There are six to ten pairs of [[vein (botany)|veins]] with whitish flattened hairs on the mid rib.<ref name="DNP"/> There are ring-like [[stipule]]s at the base of the leave stem.<ref name="NP"/> The [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] is {{cvt|0.8 to 3|cm}} long and {{cvt|1 to 2|mm}} thick, and is also covered with minute hairs.<ref name="DNP"/> The bark and leaves ooze a milky and sticky [[sap]].<ref name="Morton"/>

[[File:Artocarpus heterophylla flowers.JPG|thumb|upright=0.6|left|Flower buds]]

The tree is [[monoecious]] and produces an [[inflorescence]] from the trunk and large branches ([[cauliflory]]).<ref name="Morton"/> The male flowers are borne in clusters along the leaf axils, or smaller branches while the larger female flowers often occur on larger branches or on the trunk. The male flower bearing [[peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]s measure {{cvt|1 to 5.5|cm}} long with the female flower bearing stalks measuring longer ranging from {{cvt|3 to 10|cm}}. The male flowers are {{cvt|2.5 to 7|cm}} long and {{cvt|0.8 to 2.8|cm}} wide, and the female flowers are larger.<ref name="DNP"/>

The flowers look pale green when young and become darker later. The male flowers can be distinguished by the presence of yellow coloured [[pollen]].<ref name="CRFG">{{cite web |url=https://crfg.org/homepage/library/fruitfacts/jackfruit/ |title=Jackfruit Fruit Facts |year=1996 |publisher=California Rare Fruit Growers |access-date=3 September 2023 |archive-date=29 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229063044/https://crfg.org/homepage/library/fruitfacts/jackfruit/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[perianth]] is two lobed and rounded, and is covered with fine hairs. The [[stamen]] is {{cvt|1.5 to 2|mm}} long. [[Bract]]s may be present in between the flowers. The [[infructescence]] is {{cvt|30 to 100|cm}} long and {{cvt|25–50|cm}} wide, bearing small ellipsoid fruit heads.<ref name="DNP"/>

[[File:Jackfruit National fruit of Bangladesh.jpg|alt=Jackfruit tree with fruits|thumb|Cluster of fruits]]

The jackfruit is amongst the largest of all tree-borne fruits.<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="CRFG"/> It measures {{cvt|20 to 90|cm}} in length and {{cvt|15 to 50|cm}} in width. The matured fruits weigh anywhere between {{cvt|4.5 to 50|kg}}. The fruit is green or yellowish-green on the outer side.<ref name="Morton"/> The colour changes to brownish yellow when the fruit matures.<ref name="NP"/> The hard and rubbery outer shell has numerous thick [[tubercle]]s,<ref name="Morton"/> which somewhat flatten with maturation.<ref name="NP"/> The fully ripe fruit emits a characteristic odour,<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="NP"/> due to the presence of several [[Volatile organic compound|volatile organic compounds]] such as [[ethyl isovalerate]], propyl isovalerate, butyl isovalerate, isobutyl isovalerate, [[3-methylbutyl acetate]], [[1-butanol]], and [[2-methylbutan-1-ol]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ong |first1=B.T. |last2=Nazimah |first2=S.A.H. |last3=Tan |first3=C.P. |last4=Mirhosseini |first4=H. |last5=Osman |first5=A. |last6=Hashim |first6=D. Mat |last7=Rusul |first7=G. |date=August 2008 |title=Analysis of volatile compounds in five jackfruit (''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' L.) cultivars using solid-phase microextraction (SPME) and gas chromatography-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC-TOFMS) |url=https://www.academia.edu/15454779 |journal=[[Journal of Food Composition and Analysis]] |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=416–422 |doi=10.1016/j.jfca.2008.03.002 |archive-date=31 March 2021 |access-date=6 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331125352/https://www.academia.edu/15454779/Analysis_of_volatile_compounds_in_five_jackfruit_Artocarpus_heterophyllus_L_cultivars_using_solid_phase_microextraction_SPME_and_gas_chromatography_time_of_flight_mass_spectrometry_GC_TOFMS_ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The interior of the fruit is yellow in colour and consists of several bulbs situated amongst a cluster of narrow and sticky strips.<ref name="Morton"/> A fruit may contain 100 to 500 of these bulbs, each of which enclose a single [[seed]]. The bulbs are soft and fleshy in some varieties while it is harder in others. The brown coloured seed is {{cvt|0.75 to 1.5|in}} long and {{cvt|0.5 to 0.75|in}} thick.<ref name="CRFG"/> The smooth and elliptical shaped seed is covered by a thin white coloured seed coat.<ref name="Morton"/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Jackfruit - Flora Sinensis 1656 (2950721).jpg|thumb|upright=0.65|Illustration of jackfruit by [[Michael Boym]] {{circa|1656}}]]

The jackfruit tree is native to India and might belong to the [[Western Ghats]] range in India.<ref name="Kew"/><ref name="CRFG"/> It spread to [[Southeast Asia]], and to the islands of Indonesia and the Philippines. It was later introduced to [[East Africa]] and to the Americas.<ref name="CRFG"/> In addition to the various countries in [[South Asia]] and Southeast Asia, where it is extensively grown,<ref name="Morton"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/f_n-19.pdf |title=Jackfruit |publisher=College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources, [[University of Hawaii at Manoa]] |last1=Love |first1=Ken |last2=Paull |first2=Robert |date=June 2011 |access-date=23 May 2016 |archive-date=27 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227025333/https://www.ctahr.hawaii.edu/oc/freepubs/pdf/f_n-19.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> it is also found in China, Brazil, Suriname, and Venezuela in South America, the [[Caribbean]], [[Central Africa|Central]], East and [[West Africa]] and the islands of Mauritius, Seychelles, and Reunion,<ref name="Kew"/><ref name="CRFG"/> and parts of Oceania and North America.<ref>{{cite book |last=Boning |first=Charles R. |date=2006 |title=Florida's Best Fruiting Plants:Native and Exotic Trees, Shrubs, and Vines |location=Sarasota, Florida |publisher=Pineapple Press |page=107 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Elevitch |first1=Craig R. |last2=Manner |first2=Harley I. |chapter=''Artocarpus heterophyllus'' (Jackfruit) |editor1-first=Craig R. |editor1-last=Elevitch |title=Traditional Trees of Pacific Islands: Their Culture, Environment, and Use |date=2006 |publisher=Permanent Agriculture Resources |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2Grw4g0-h54C&pg=PT127 |isbn=978-0-970-25445-0 |page=112 }}</ref> It can become an [[invasive species]] as in Brazil's [[Tijuca Forest]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Danger or delight? Uphill battle for Brazil's huge jackfruit |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Lifestyle/wireStory/danger-delight-uphill-battle-brazils-huge-jackfruit-76182430 |work=ABC News |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=5 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705220808/https://abcnews.go.com/Lifestyle/wireStory/danger-delight-uphill-battle-brazils-huge-jackfruit-76182430 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The jackfruit tree grows in a variety of habitats ranging from [[tropical rainforest]] to lowland and [[dry forest]]s.<ref name="TBA"/> It generally grows at lower altitudes (less than {{cvt|1600|m}}),<ref name="TBA"/> and trees growing in higher altitudes tend to produce low quality fruits.<ref name="Morton"/> It requires optimal temperature between {{cvt|19 to 29|C}} with sunlight. It is not [[drought resistant]] beyond a few months and requires adequate moisture.<ref name="TBA"/><ref name="CRFG"/> Though it grows in various soil types, it grows well in slightly acidic, moist and well drained soils.<ref name="TBA"/><ref name="CRFG"/> In India, it has been observed to grow thicker and stouter on conducive soils and thinner in sandy soils.<ref name="Morton"/>

==Reproduction and lifespan==
The plant is generally grown from the seed, though it can be grown from stem cuttings and grafts. The first shoots arise anywhere between 10 to 40 days depending on the conditions.<ref name="CRFG"/><ref name="NP"/> The plant can be transplanted in the initial few weeks.<ref name="CRFG"/> The tree matures and may start bearing fruits anywhere between 4 to 14 years though earlier occurrences have been noted. It reaches its maximum height around 20 years. In suitable conditions, the tree has a productive lifespan of more than a hundred years, though the yield might reduce or stop with ageing.<ref name="Morton"/> Insects help in [[pollination]] with a three-way mutualism involving the tree, a fungus, and a species of [[gall midge]], ''Clinidiplosis ultracrepidata'', has been noted. The fungus forms a film which is a food source for the insects.<ref>{{cite book |last=Balcombe |first=Jonathan |title=Super Fly: The Unexpected Lives of the World's Most Successful Insects |date=2021 |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |isbn=978-0-143-13427-5 |location=New York |page=152}}</ref>

==Cultivation and production==

The jackfruit is extensively cultivated commercially in South and Southeast Asia, and other parts of the world such as Brazil.<ref name="CRFG"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.seagri.ba.gov.br/jaca.htm |title=Jaca |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090413050157/http://www.seagri.ba.gov.br/jaca.htm |archive-date=13 April 2009 |work=Department of Agriculture, [[State of Bahia]]}}</ref> Archaeological evidence has revealed that the jackfruit was cultivated in India about 3,000 to 6,000 years ago.<ref>{{cite book |date=2011 |editor1-last=Preedy |editor1-first=Victor R. |editor2-last=Watson |editor2-first=Ronald Ross |editor3-last=Patel |editor3-first=Vinood B. |title=Nuts and Seeds in Health and Disease Prevention |url=https://archive.org/details/nutsseedshealthd00pree |url-access=limited |edition=1st |location=Burlington, Massachusetts |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/nutsseedshealthd00pree/page/n1092 678] |isbn=978-0-123-75689-3 }}</ref> Though there are several cultivars and varities,<ref name="CRFG"/> two broad types of fruits are generally described, one with soft, juicy, and sweet kernels, and the other with hard and crisp ones.<ref name="Morton"/> The fruits mature three to eight months after flowering.<ref name="CRFG"/> It is harvested by hand, and ripe fruits turn colour from pale green to greenish brown, give a characteristic odour, and makes a hollow noise when tapped.<ref name="CRFG"/><ref name="NP"/>

Once harvested, the fruit has to be consumed quickly, and once cut open, they deteriorate within a few days. At cooler temperatures, the fruits can survive three to six weeks.<ref name="CRFG"/> As per an estimate, about 75% of the fruits go waste due to the limited life span.<ref name="WA"/> Due to the presence of [[latex]], the hands, knives, and other surfaces are generally quoted with a viscous liquid like oil to prevent sticking.<ref name="CRFG"/> Fresh jackfruit can be found commonly at food markets throughout South and Southeast Asia.<ref name="Goldenberg">{{cite web |last=Goldenberg |first=Suzanne |date=23 April 2014 |title=Jackfruit heralded as 'miracle' food crop |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/apr/23/jackfruit-miracle-crop-climate-change-food-security |access-date=17 October 2016 |work=[[The Guardian]] |archive-date=8 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108111555/http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/apr/23/jackfruit-miracle-crop-climate-change-food-security |url-status=live }}</ref> The fruit is sold as whole, in slices, or as individual bulbs. The seeds are also dried and sold separately for consumption.<ref name="CRFG"/> Apart from fresh fruit, the fruit is also sold as frozen, dried, or canned, or processed into other foods.<ref name="Goldenberg"/><ref>{{cite web |first=Brian |last=Kateman |date=20 August 2019 |title=This Ancient 'Miracle Fruit' Is The Latest Meat Replacement Craze |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/briankateman/2019/08/20/this-ancient-miracle-fruit-is-the-latest-meat-replacement-craze/#1ef039dc7977 |access-date=2 September 2019 |work=[[Forbes]] |archive-date=8 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308064301/https://www.forbes.com/sites/briankateman/2019/08/20/this-ancient-miracle-fruit-is-the-latest-meat-replacement-craze/#1ef039dc7977 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2024, India was the largest producer with 1.436 million [[tonnes]] of jackfruit, followed by Bangladesh (0.926 mt), Thailand (0.392 mt), and Indonesia (0.340 mt).<ref name="WA">{{cite web |title=World Leaders In Jackfruit Production |url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/world-leaders-in-jackfruit-production.html |access-date=14 June 2026 |publisher=World Atlas |archive-date=8 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308211140/https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/world-leaders-in-jackfruit-production.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The edible raw pulp is 74% water, 23% [[carbohydrate]]s, 2% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and 1% [[fat]] (table). The carbohydrate component is primarily sugars, and is a source of [[dietary fiber]]. In a reference amount of {{convert|100|g}}, raw jackfruit provides 95 [[kilocalorie]]s, and is a moderate source (10–19% of the [[Daily Value]]) of [[vitamin B6|vitamin B<sub>6</sub>]], [[vitamin C]], and [[potassium in biology|potassium]], with no appreciable content of other [[micronutrient]]s (table).

==Culinary==
The jackfruit is widely consumed in South and South East Asia, and is considered a partial solution for [[food security]] in [[Least Developed Countries|developing countries]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Silver |first1=Mark |title=Here's The Scoop On Jackfruit, A Ginormous Fruit To Feed The World |work=NPR |date=May 2014 |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2014/05/01/308708000/heres-the-scoop-on-jackfruit-a-ginormous-fruit-to-feed-the-world |access-date=19 April 2016 |archive-date=27 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127045201/https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2014/05/01/308708000/heres-the-scoop-on-jackfruit-a-ginormous-fruit-to-feed-the-world |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/business/article/2000106577/venture-in-rare-jackfruit-turns-farmer-s-fortunes-around |title=Venture in rare jackfruit turns farmers' fortunes around |work=Standard Online |last=Mwandambo |first=Pascal |date=11 March 2014 |access-date=20 December 2016 |archive-date=21 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221091556/https://www.standardmedia.co.ke/business/article/2000106577/venture-in-rare-jackfruit-turns-farmer-s-fortunes-around |url-status=live }}</ref> The ripe fruit gives a sweet, with subtle pineapple- or banana-like flavor.<ref name="Morton"/> The fruit bulbs are often eaten when ripe while both ripe and raw fruits are used in cuisine.<ref name="WA"/> Raw fruits can be [[pickling|pickled]] in [[brine]] or dry fruits and fruit pulp can be preserved.<ref name="Morton"/> The canned fruit can be preserved for up to an year and is marked as a [[meat alternative]].<ref name="Morton"/><ref>{{cite web |last=Stukin |first=Stacie |title=Is Jackfruit the Next Big Meat Substitute? |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/jackfruit-sustainable-vegetarian-meat-substitute |date=15 July 2016 |publisher=[[National Geographic]] |url-access=registration |access-date=15 March 2025 |archive-date=18 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250318105716/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/jackfruit-sustainable-vegetarian-meat-substitute |url-status=live }}</ref> The fruit pulp can be stored up to two years under suitable temperature.<ref name="Morton"/>

The ripe jackfruit is used to make a variety of sweet dishes and [[desserts]]. It is made into jams, jellies, and mixed with sugar or honey to make candies and beverages.<ref name="NP"/><ref name="WA"/> In India, the dried bulbs are fried in oil to make chips.<ref name="Morton"/> The fruit bulbs can be [[fermented]] and [[distilled]] to produce liquor.<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="NP"/> Unripe jackfruit is used in various South Asian and South East Asian cuisine to make [[curry]] and other dishes.<ref>{{cite book |date=2007|pages=155; 175; 481–5 |title=The encyclopedia of fruit and nuts |last1=Janick |first1=Jules |last2=Paull |first2=Robert E. |isbn=978-0-851-99638-7|oclc=1114741519}}</ref><ref name="DS">{{cite web |last1=Matin |first1=Abdul |title=A poor man's fruit: Now a miracle food! |url=http://www.thedailystar.net/a-poor-mans-fruit-now-a-miracle-food-41297 |work=[[The Daily Star (Bangladesh)|The Daily Star]] |access-date=12 June 2015 |archive-date=25 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225203858/https://www.thedailystar.net/a-poor-mans-fruit-now-a-miracle-food-41297 |url-status=live }}</ref> It is cooked with [[coconut milk]] to improve the flavor.<ref name="WA"/> 

The seeds have a creamy taste, and are usually boiled or roasted before usage.<ref name="WA"/> It can be dried and salted and eaten as a snack.<ref name="NP"/> The seeds are also ground to [[flour]] which is used while making breads.<ref name="NP"/> The roasted seeds are also used as a commercial alternative to [[cocoa bean]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Spada |first1=Fernanda Papa |display-authors=etal |title=Optimization of Postharvest Conditions To Produce Chocolate Aroma from Jackfruit Seeds |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |date=21 January 2017 |volume=65 |issue=6 |pages=1196–1208 |doi=10.1021/acs.jafc.6b04836 |pmid=28110526 |bibcode=2017JAFC...65.1196S |url=http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/68248/1/FINAL%20Paper%20Jack%20I%20-22nd%20Jan%202017.pdf |archive-date=28 February 2021 |access-date=14 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210228144217/http://centaur.reading.ac.uk/68248/1/FINAL%20Paper%20Jack%20I%20-22nd%20Jan%202017.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Other uses ==
Jackfruit bark, pulp, and seeds have been used in [[traditional medicine]].<ref name="Morton"/> In traditional medicine, it is used as a natural coolant and an antidote to alcohol. The roots are used for the treatment of [[fever]], [[asthma]], [[diarrhea]], and [[skin diseases]], and the leaves are used as an [[antiseptic]] to treat wounds. The bark is used as an [[anesthetic]] and the ash is mixed with other ingredients such as [[coconut oil]] to treat [[ulcers]]. The seeds and the dried sap are considered as [[aphrodisiac]]s, and the sap is mixed with [[vinegar]] to make an antidote to [[snakebite]].<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="NP"/>

The tree leaves are eaten by [[cattle]] and other [[herbivorous]] grazing animals. The tree also shelters birds, and a range of insects.<ref name="TBA"/> After extracting the fruit bulbs, the remnants are often used as [[fodder]].<ref name="WA"/> The leaves may be attached together to be used as plates to serve food or wrap food items.<ref name="Morton"/> The sap from the tree is used as a disinfectant due to its [[bacteria|bacterial]] resistance. The [[latex]] is also heated to make a glue, which is used to mend utensils, and boats. It is also mixed with other oils and used as [[birdlime]].<ref name="Morton"/>

Jackfruit tree wood is [[termite]] and fungi resistant and is used extensively in [[furniture]] making and construction. It is used to make [[oar]]s, wooden barrels, tools, and other implements.<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="NP"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.baodanang.vn/english/danang-attractions/201402/nam-o-fish-sauce-village-2310357/ |title=Nam O fish sauce village |work=Danang Today |date=26 February 2014 |access-date=22 September 2015 |archive-date=28 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928035416/https://baodanang.vn/english/danang-attractions/201402/nam-o-fish-sauce-village-2310357/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The wood is also used for making [[Buddha]] statues in monasteries.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://nhagoviethung.com/viewproduct/1817_gomitnai.htm |title=Gỗ mít nài |work=Nhagoviethung.com |access-date=17 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170403221851/http://nhagoviethung.com/viewproduct/1817_gomitnai.htm |archive-date=3 April 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is also used extensively to make [[musical instrument]]s,<ref name="Morton"/><ref name="NP"/> including the Indian string instrument ''[[veena]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chauhan |first1=Chandrashekhar |last2=Singru |first2=P. M. |last3=Vathsan |first3=Radhika |date=31 March 2021 |title=The effect of the extended bridge on the Timbre of the Sarasvati Veena: a numerical and experimental study |journal=Journal of Measurements in Engineering |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=23–35 |doi=10.21595/jme.2020.21712 |issn=2335-2124 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Wood splinters are used to collect [[Palm toddy|toddy]] from [[coconut]] trees. Dry twigs and branches are used during [[homa (ritual)|homa]] rituals in [[Hinduism]].<ref name="Morton"/> A cloth dye is extracted from the tree bark.<ref name="NP"/> The saw dust and wooden fragments are used to create a yellow dye used to colour the [[cotton]] robes of [[Buddhist]] monks.<ref name="Morton"/>

==Culture and symbolism==

|url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/politics-and-nation/jack-fruit-to-be-keralas-state-fruit-declaration-on-mar-21/articleshow/63344035.cms |access-date=17 March 2018 |work=[[The Economic Times]] |archive-date=8 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308203527/https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/politics-and-nation/jack-fruit-to-be-keralas-state-fruit-declaration-on-mar-21/articleshow/63344035.cms |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[List of Tamil Nadu state symbols|Tamil Nadu]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://wiienvis.nic.in/KidsCentre/state_symbols_india_8411.aspx|title=State Symbols of India|publisher=[[Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change]], [[Government of India]]|access-date=30 August 2023|archive-date=22 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230922102907/https://wiienvis.nic.in/KidsCentre/state_symbols_india_8411.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://tnbb.tn.gov.in/state-symbol.php|title=Symbols of Tamil Nadu|publisher=[[Government of Tamil Nadu]]|access-date=12 August 2023|archive-date=31 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240331152841/https://tnbb.tn.gov.in/state-symbol.php|url-status=live}}</ref>
